chunks.title: Classifying uveitis (SUN)
chunks.tldr: By site: anterior (AC), intermediate (vitreous, pars planitis), posterior (retina/choroid), panuveitis. By cause: infectious, non-infectious, masquerade.
points: SUN timing: onset sudden/insidious. Duration limited (≤3 months) or persistent.
Acute = sudden + limited. Recurrent = episodes with untreated quiet gaps. Chronic = persistent, relapses <3 months after stopping treatment.
Remission = no cells for ≥3 months.
Anterior uveitis is the commonest. Iritis ≈ iridocyclitis clinically.
AAU: mostly HLA-B27 or idiopathic. Also trauma, surgery, lens, HSV, keratitis, scleritis, sarcoid.
CAU: more often bilateral, more systemic disease, often granulomatous.
~50% of anterior uveitis has no systemic cause. HLA-B27 ~20% of AAU. Others: VZV, TB, syphilis, Lyme, JIA, sarcoid, Behçet, TINU, SLE, MS, drugs, masquerade (lymphoma, melanoma, JXG).
chunks.hook: Uveitis map: Front, Middle, Back, Everywhere.

cards.q: SUN definition of chronic uveitis?
cards.a: Persistent uveitis with relapse within 3 months of stopping treatment.

cards.q: Proportion of AAU that is HLA-B27 related?
cards.a: About 20% (≈50% of otherwise healthy AAU patients are B27+).

chunks.title: Anterior uveitis signs
chunks.tldr: AAU: painful red photophobic eye, ciliary flush, small pupil, cells + flare, KPs. Mutton-fat KPs + iris nodules = granulomatous. Stellate diffuse KPs = Fuchs.
points: Ciliary injection (purple ring at the limbus), miosis (→ synechiae).
AC cells (count before dilating) in a 1×1 mm beam: 0 <1, 0.5+ 1–5, 1+ 6–15, 2+ 16–25, 3+ 26–50, 4+ >50.
Flare (protein): 1+ faint, 2+ moderate (iris clear), 3+ marked (iris hazy), 4+ fibrin. Flare = active disease (JIA data).
Hypopyon: B27 (fibrin-rich, fixed) vs Behçet (shifts with head position).
KPs: inferior Arlt triangle. Small = non-granulomatous. Large greasy 'mutton fat' = granulomatous. Stellate, diffuse = Fuchs.
Fibrin in AC → B27.
Iris nodules: Koeppe (pupil edge), Busacca (stroma, granulomatous). Roseolae (syphilis), pearls (leprosy), Russell bodies (crystals).
Posterior synechiae → dilate early. Iris atrophy: diffuse (Fuchs), sectoral/patchy (herpes).
Heterochromia (Fuchs). Iris NV (chronic). IOP low (shutdown) or high.
Always examine the fundus: masquerades, posterior disease, CMO.
chunks.hook: Mutton fat = Many causes that are granulomatous (sarcoid, TB, syphilis, VKH, SO).

cards.q: Hypopyon that shifts with head position?
Iris nodules at the pupil margin vs in the stroma?
SUN grade for 20 cells in a 1×1 mm beam?

chunks.title: Posterior uveitis signs
chunks.tldr: Retinitis = fluffy white retina with fuzzy edges (vitritis). Choroiditis = round yellow nodule (little vitritis). Vasculitis = white sheathing (veins > arteries).
points: Symptoms depend on location: periphery → floaters; macula → central blur.
Retinitis: focal, multifocal, geographic or diffuse. White with oedematous edges → sharpens as it heals.
Choroiditis: yellow nodule, little vitreous reaction unless the retina is involved.
Vasculitis: periphlebitis (commoner) or periarteritis. Yellow-grey cuffing ± haemorrhage. Old scars ≠ active.
Often both: retinochoroiditis (retina first, e.g. toxo) or chorioretinitis (choroid first).
chunks.hook: Retinitis = fluffy cloud. Choroiditis = yellow button.

cards.q: Does choroiditis alone usually cause much vitritis?

chunks.title: Who to investigate & which tests
chunks.tldr: Single mild unilateral non-granulomatous AAU → no tests. Recurrent, severe, bilateral, granulomatous, chronic or posterior → test. Core: HLA-B27, syphilis serology, ACE, CXR, QuantiFERON.
points: Skip tests: first mild one-sided AAU, classic Fuchs, known cause (e.g. sarcoid).
Test: recurrent, severe, bilateral, persistent/chronic, granulomatous, with intermediate/posterior disease, systemic clues.
HLA-B27 (chromosome 6). Positive in 50% of healthy AAU, 90% of AAU with spondyloarthropathy.
HLA links: A29 = birdshot, B51 = Behçet, B7/DR2 = POHS, DR4 = sympathetic ophthalmia & VKH.
Syphilis: treponemal test (ELISA, very sensitive) + non-treponemal (RPR/VDRL, tracks activity). Do both.
ACE (sarcoid ~80% active; high in normal kids, exercise), lysozyme.
ESR/CRP, FBC (infection, eosinophils), Lyme, ANA (kids/JIA), ANCA (with scleritis/PUK), QuantiFERON, HIV (opportunistic).
X-ray: sacroiliac (AS), chest (sarcoid, TB).
Imaging: B-scan, OCT (CMO), FAF (white dots), FA (vasculitis, ischaemia), ICGA (choroid), UBM (hypotony).
Aqueous PCR: HSV, VZV, CMV, rubella (hypertensive or steroid-resistant AU), P. acnes. Vitreous/chorioretinal biopsy for obscure posterior disease.
chunks.hook: A29 = birdshot. B51 = Behçet. DR4 = VKH/SO.

cards.q: HLA type associated with birdshot retinochoroiditis?
Which two syphilis test types should be done?

chunks.title: Treating anterior uveitis
chunks.tldr: Topical steroid (hourly → taper over ~6 weeks) + cycloplegic. Stuck synechiae → Mydricaine. Thick fibrin → intracameral tPA. CMO → periocular/intravitreal steroid.
points: Pred 1% / dex 0.1% first choice. Difluprednate (strong), loteprednol (less IOP rise), FML/rimexolone (weaker). Ointment at night.
AAU taper: hourly 3 days → 2-hourly 3 days → QID 1 week → TDS → BD → OD → stop (~5–6 weeks). Review after stopping.
CAU: aim for zero cells and flare (except Fuchs).
Steroid risks: IOP rise, cataract, infection, HSV, melt. Kids: systemic absorption (punctal pressure).
Cycloplegics: cyclopentolate (12–24 h) < homatropine (3 days) < atropine (7–10 days). + phenylephrine to break synechiae. Kids: toxicity, amblyopia.
Mydricaine No. 2 (adrenaline + atropine + procaine) subconj or on a pledget → breaks fresh synechiae (monitor heart).
tPA 12.5–25 µg intracameral for heavy fibrin.
Subconj betamethasone for severe/poor compliance.
Orbital floor / posterior sub-Tenon triamcinolone (40 mg): CMO, non-compliance. Peak 4 weeks, lasts ~3 months. Risks: IOP (up to 25%), perforation, ptosis, cataract.
Intravitreal triamcinolone 4 mg or slow-release implants for stubborn CMO.
Oral steroid rarely; NSAIDs long-term for CAU; methotrexate for JIA etc.
chunks.hook: Steroid to calm, cycloplegic to stop sticking.

cards.q: Duration of action of atropine cycloplegia?
What can dissolve dense fibrin in the AC?

chunks.title: Immunomodulators for uveitis
chunks.tldr: Goal: steroid-free remission. Start immediately for Behçet or SLE with retinal vasculitis; early for SO, VKH, birdshot, serpiginous, MCP, JIA. Exclude TB first.
points: Multidisciplinary team. Consent, exclude infection (esp. TB), check blood/kidney/liver.
Immediate: Behçet and SLE with retinal vasculitis.
Early: sympathetic ophthalmia, VKH, birdshot, serpiginous, MFC/panuveitis, JIA.
As steroid alternative: failing/intolerant, needing >0.5 mg/kg pred, sight-threatening/chronic disease, exudative RD, macular involvement.
Antimetabolites: methotrexate, mycophenolate, azathioprine.
Calcineurin inhibitors: ciclosporin, tacrolimus, voclosporin, sirolimus.
Alkylating: cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil.
Anti-TNF: adalimumab, infliximab, etanercept, golimumab, certolizumab. Take 2 weeks–3 months → bridge with steroids.
Common immunosuppressants don't raise cancer mortality at these doses; azathioprine or anti-TNF alone → tiny lymphoma risk (higher combined).
chunks.hook: Behçet/SLE vasculitis = start NOW.

cards.q: Two conditions needing immediate immunomodulatory therapy?
cards.a: Behçet disease and SLE with retinal vasculitis.

cards.q: Infection to exclude before anti-TNF therapy?

chunks.title: Spondyloarthropathies: AS, reactive, psoriatic
chunks.tldr: HLA-B27 family. Ankylosing spondylitis: young man, morning back stiffness, AAU in 25% (alternating eyes). Reactive arthritis: can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree.
points: Seronegative (no RF), B27, enthesitis. Group: AS, undifferentiated, psoriatic, reactive, IBD arthritis.
AS: men, 90% B27+. Low back/buttock pain and stiffness in their 20s–30s, bamboo spine, sacroiliitis on X-ray (can precede symptoms).
AS eye: AAU 25% (25% of men with AAU have AS). Either eye at different times, rarely both together. Also scleritis, episcleritis.
Reactive arthritis (Reiter): 1–4 weeks after urethritis (Chlamydia) or gut infection (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter). ~75% B27+.
Reactive: urethritis + conjunctivitis + arthritis (knees, ankles, toes), enthesitis (plantar fasciitis, Achilles, heel spur), keratoderma blennorrhagica, circinate balanitis, mouth ulcers.
Reactive eye: bilateral mucopurulent conjunctivitis (very common, self-limiting), AAU 20%, keratitis.
Psoriatic arthritis: up to 40% of psoriasis. Nail pitting, onycholysis, DIP / sausage digits. AAU ~7%.
Biologics (infliximab) endorsed for chronic sight-threatening uveitis.
chunks.hook: Reiter: Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree.

cards.q: Percentage of AS patients who get AAU?
Skin lesion on palms/soles in reactive arthritis?

chunks.title: Fuchs uveitis syndrome
chunks.tldr: White eye, one side, heterochromia, diffuse stellate KPs, no synechiae, iris atrophy, cataract, vitreous floaters, glaucoma. Rubella link. Steroids don't help chronic low-grade disease.
points: Average age ~40. 90–95% one eye. Possibly rubella (or toxo).
Presents with blur (PSC cataract) or floaters.
Heterochromia: usually affected eye lighter (blue eyes may get darker as stroma thins). Subtle in brown eyes.
No posterior synechiae (except after surgery). Eye is always white.
Stellate grey-white KPs over the whole endothelium.
Koeppe nodules, Russell bodies, smooth featureless iris, fine iris vessels.
Vitritis can be dense. Glaucoma up to 60%.
Gonio: fine angle vessels → Amsler sign (bleed when AC entered). No CMO except after surgery.
Treatment: monitor. Steroids only for bad flares. Cataract surgery: more bleeding, inflammation, glaucoma. Glaucoma: tube/trab+MMC. PPV for floaters.
chunks.hook: Fuchs: White, one-sided, stellate KPs, no synechiae, lighter iris.

cards.q: Bleeding from angle vessels on entering the AC in Fuchs uveitis?
Name 3 causes of hyperchromic heterochromia.
cards.a: Unilateral prostaglandin use, naevus of Ota, siderosis (also iris naevus/melanoma, Sturge–Weber).

chunks.title: JIA uveitis
chunks.tldr: Commonest cause of childhood uveitis. Silent white eye, chronic, both eyes. Highest risk: oligoarticular, ANA+, girl, onset <7. Must screen (every 3–4 months). Complications: band keratopathy, cataract, glaucoma.
points: JIA = arthritis <16 years lasting ≥6 weeks. ~1 in 1000.
Oligoarticular (≤4 joints, knees): commonest, girls 5:1, peak age 2, 75% ANA+ → uveitis ~20%.
Polyarticular RF−: uveitis 5–10%. Polyarticular RF+: very low risk.
Systemic (Still): fever, rash, nodes, organ enlargement → uveitis rare.
Enthesitis-related and psoriatic: relatively high risk.
Uveitis: no symptoms, no redness even with 4+ cells. Chronic non-granulomatous, both eyes (70%), endothelial dusting, no hypopyon.
Found late by parents: squint, white pupil (cataract), band on the cornea.
Complications: PS, band keratopathy, cataract, glaucoma, amblyopia, CMO, ERM, cyclitic membrane, phthisis.
Screening: first exam within 6 weeks. 2-monthly for 6 months (high-risk groups), then 3–4 monthly until ~12. Chase missed appointments. Self-check vision weekly after discharge.
Differentials: idiopathic CAU, reactive/IBD arthritis, juvenile sarcoid, Lyme, intermediate uveitis, NOMID, retinoblastoma masquerade, Blau syndrome.
Treat: topical steroid (works in 80%), short-acting mydriatic (amblyopia), early methotrexate → adalimumab/infliximab. Avoid etanercept (worsens uveitis).
Glaucoma: trab + MMC (better on anti-TNF), Baerveldt. Cataract surgery + IOL OK if well controlled.
chunks.hook: JIA eye = quiet but dangerous. No symptoms ≠ no disease.

cards.q: Highest-risk JIA subtype for uveitis?
Which anti-TNF should be avoided in JIA uveitis?

chunks.title: Bowel & kidney: UC, Crohn, Whipple, TINU
chunks.tldr: IBD → AAU (UC ~5%, Crohn 3%) + episcleritis/scleritis. Whipple (Tropheryma) → uveitis + oculomasticatory myorhythmia. TINU = teenage girl, kidney inflammation + bilateral AU.
points: Ulcerative colitis: rectum upwards, continuous ulcers, bloody diarrhoea, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, sclerosing cholangitis. AAU ~5% (with flares; more if B27/arthritis). Episcleritis, scleritis.
Crohn: mouth to anus, skip lesions, full-thickness granulomas, fistulae. CARD15/NOD2. Eye inflammation 12% (AAU 3%, episcleritis, scleritis, myositis, optic neuritis).

Whipple disease: Tropheryma whipplei, middle-aged white men, malabsorption + joints + heart + brain. Eye: keratitis, uveitis, retinitis, choroiditis; gaze palsy, oculomasticatory myorhythmia. Curable with antibiotics.
TINU: adolescent girls, kidney disease first (proteinuria, renal failure), then bilateral AU (sometimes posterior). Responds to steroids, may relapse.
IgA nephropathy: haematuria after URTI, rare AAU.
chunks.hook: Teen girl + kidneys + both eyes inflamed = TINU.

cards.q: Bilateral anterior uveitis in an adolescent girl with renal failure?
Pathognomonic eye–jaw movement sign in Whipple disease?

chunks.title: Intermediate uveitis & pars planitis
chunks.tldr: Floaters + blur, white eye. Snowballs (inferior vitreous), snowbanking (pars plana), periphlebitis. Main vision threat = CMO. Rule out MS, sarcoid, Lyme, syphilis, TB.
points: Vitreous = main site. Up to 15% of uveitis, 20% in kids. 'Pars planitis' only if idiopathic with snowballs/banks.
Insidious blur + floaters, no pain/redness. Usually both eyes (asymmetric).
Few AC cells (more in kids, sarcoid, Lyme). Anterior vitreous cells. Haze graded 0–4 by how well you see NFL/disc.
Snowballs (inferior), periphlebitis (esp. MS), snowbank (inferior grey-white plaque).
Peripheral/disc NV → vitreous haemorrhage (kids), vasoproliferative tumour.
Disc swelling, CMO (up to 50%), ERM, cataract, glaucoma, RD (can → phthisis).
75% keep ≥6/12 at 4 years.
Tests: ESR/CRP, FBC, OCT, FA. MS (MRI if any symptoms; women 20–50), sarcoid (ACE, CXR), Lyme, syphilis, TB before steroids. Mimics: Fuchs, lymphoma (elderly), toxocara, Whipple, Candida, toxo.

Treat: topical steroid (anterior only), periocular steroid (4–6 injections), NSAID, cryo or laser to snowbank/ischaemic retina, intravitreal steroid/implants, oral pred 1–2 mg/kg, immunosuppressants, interferon-β (MS), infliximab.
PPV: tractional RD, ERM, refractory CMO, dense opacities, haemorrhage, peripheral NV.
chunks.hook: Snowballs + snowbanks = winter in the vitreous. Check for MS.

cards.q: Main cause of reduced vision in intermediate uveitis?
Neurological disease to consider in intermediate uveitis with periphlebitis?

chunks.title: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH)
chunks.tldr: Autoimmune attack on melanocytes (eye, ear, skin, meninges). Asian/Hispanic/dark skin, HLA-DR4. Headache/tinnitus → bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with multifocal exudative RDs → later sunset-glow fundus, vitiligo, poliosis.
points: Phases: prodrome (meningism, tinnitus, vertigo, deafness, CN palsies) → acute uveitic (bilateral granulomatous AU + choroiditis, Dalen–Fuchs nodules, papillitis, multifocal serous RDs, ciliary effusion) → convalescent (alopecia, poliosis, vitiligo, sunset glow, Sugiura sign at the limbus) → chronic recurrent (anterior uveitis flares).
Diagnostic criteria: (1) no penetrating trauma, (2) no other eye disease, (3) bilateral uveitis, (4) neuro/auditory, (5) skin signs. Complete = all 5. Incomplete = 1–3 + 4 or 5. Probable = 1–3.
Complications: CNV, subretinal fibrosis, NV, cataract, glaucoma.

Tests: LP (lymphocytes, melanin macrophages), FAF, B-scan (thick choroid; excludes posterior scleritis), FA (pinpoint leaks → pooling), OCT (subretinal septae), ICGA (hypofluorescent spots; monitoring).
Treat: high-dose oral pred 1–2 mg/kg (± IV methylpred) tapered over 3–6 months. Early immunosuppression/infliximab if not responding.
chunks.hook: VKH = Very Krazy Hair (white lashes, bald patches) + exudative RDs.

cards.q: Name 3 convalescent-phase signs of VKH.
cards.a: Sunset glow fundus, vitiligo, poliosis (also alopecia, Sugiura sign).

cards.q: Typical FA in acute VKH?
cards.a: Multiple pinpoint hyperfluorescent leaks at the RPE followed by subretinal pooling.

chunks.title: Sympathetic ophthalmia & lens-induced uveitis
chunks.tldr: SO = bilateral granulomatous panuveitis 2 weeks–3 months after penetrating injury (or multiple VR surgeries) to one eye. Dalen–Fuchs nodules. Enucleate a hopeless eye within 10–14 days. Treat with high-dose steroids + early immunosuppression.
points: ~0.2–0.5% after injury, 0.01% after surgery. HLA links (DR4).
Histology: diffuse lymphocytes in the choroid, melanin-containing epithelioid cells, Dalen–Fuchs nodules (between Bruch and RPE; also VKH).
Exciting eye (injured) red and irritable. Sympathising eye: blur, photophobia, loss of accommodation.
Bilateral granulomatous AU, midperipheral multifocal choroidal infiltrates, exudative RD, vasculitis, disc swelling → later sunset glow.
75% keep >6/60 with aggressive treatment. Relapse 50% (can be years later).
Prevent: enucleation within 10–14 days of injury in a blind eye (evisceration OK if all uvea removed).
Treat: high-dose oral steroid ± IV methylpred, topical/periocular/intravitreal adjuncts, early immunosuppression.

Lens-induced (phacoantigenic) uveitis: immune reaction to exposed lens protein (retained fragments after phaco, trauma, leaky mature lens). Granulomatous AU, corneal oedema near AC fragments, high IOP, vitritis. Steroids + remove the lens material (small posterior bits may absorb). Must tell from endophthalmitis.
chunks.hook: One eye injured → both eyes inflamed = sympathetic ophthalmia.

cards.q: Typical time from injury to sympathetic ophthalmia?
Where are Dalen–Fuchs nodules located?
cards.a: Between Bruch membrane and the RPE.

chunks.title: Sarcoidosis: body
chunks.tldr: Non-caseating granulomas, mostly lungs + lymph nodes. More in black people. Löfgren = erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + arthralgia (good prognosis).
points: Black:white ~10:1, colder climates. One of the commonest systemic causes of uveitis.
Cough, breathlessness, malaise, arthralgia (~50% each). Some found on routine CXR or via uveitis.
Löfgren syndrome: erythema nodosum + BHL + polyarthralgia (usually women).
Lungs: infiltrates → fibrosis.
Skin (25%): erythema nodosum, lupus pernio (purple nose/cheeks/ears), papules.
Neuro: meningitis, cranial nerve palsies, pituitary. Heart (5%): arrhythmia, sudden death.
Enlarged lymph nodes.
chunks.hook: Sarcoid = granulomas without cheese (non-caseating).

cards.q: Triad of Löfgren syndrome?
cards.a: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, polyarthralgia.

chunks.title: Sarcoidosis: eye & diagnosis
chunks.tldr: IWOS 7 signs: mutton-fat KPs/iris nodules, TM nodules/tent PAS, snowballs/string of pearls, peripheral chorioretinal lesions, periphlebitis ('candle wax drippings'), disc/choroidal granuloma, bilateral. Tests: ACE, lysozyme, CXR (BHL), LFTs, chest CT, negative TB skin test.
points: Eye inflammation in 25–70%. Granulomatous AU commonest. AAU (acute sarcoid), CAU (older, chronic lung disease).
Signs: mutton-fat KPs, Koeppe/Busacca nodules, trabecular nodules, tent-shaped PAS, snowballs / string of pearls, multiple peripheral choroidal lesions (punched-out), retinal granulomas.
Periphlebitis with 'candle wax drippings', occlusion → peripheral NV (can look like sickle retinopathy), macroaneurysm.
Disc granuloma, persistent disc oedema, papilloedema (CNS).
Also: conjunctival nodules, lacrimal gland enlargement, dry eye, lid/orbital/scleral lesions.
Complications: cataract, glaucoma, synechiae, band keratopathy, CMO, ERM, CNV, RD, phthisis.
IWOS tests: negative tuberculin (in BCG/previously positive), ↑ ACE/lysozyme, CXR BHL (abnormal in 90%), abnormal LFTs, chest CT if CXR normal.
Biopsy (usually needed before treating): bronchoscopy, EBUS, skin, nodes, conjunctival nodule, lacrimal gland (75% +), vitreous (CD4/CD8). Also PET, gallium, calcium, BAL CD4/CD8.
Certainty: definite (biopsy), presumed (BHL), probable, possible.
Treat: stepwise like idiopathic uveitis; posterior → systemic steroids ± methotrexate/azathioprine/adalimumab; laser ischaemic retina; NSAID for CMO; quiet ≥3 months before surgery.
chunks.hook: Sarcoid retina = candle wax dripping down the veins.

cards.q: 'Candle wax drippings' along retinal veins?
Tuberculin skin test result typical in sarcoidosis?

chunks.title: Behçet disease
chunks.tldr: Silk Road (Turkey → Japan), HLA-B51, young men. Mouth ulcers + genital ulcers + skin + pathergy. Eye: shifting hypopyon in a white eye, occlusive retinal vasculitis (arteries + veins). Needs early immunosuppression.
points: Vasculitis of all vessel sizes. Mortality ~5% at 5–10 years (CNS/vascular). Peak age 20s–30s.

ISGBD criteria: oral ulcers ≥3/year + 2 of: genital ulcers, eye inflammation, skin lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, acneiform), positive pathergy test (pustule 24–48 h after needle prick).
Also: aneurysms, venous thrombosis, arthritis, dermatographia, neuro (brainstem, sinus thrombosis), gut.
Eye in ~70% (worse in men), eventually bilateral. Relapsing panuveitis + retinal vasculitis.
Non-granulomatous AAU with mobile hypopyon in a fairly white eye.
Vitritis. Transient white retinal infiltrates that heal without scars. Deeper viral-like retinitis.
Vasculitis: arteries AND veins (sarcoid = veins only), haemorrhages, occlusion, oedema, CMO. Main cause of vision loss.
End-stage: optic atrophy, ghost vessels, retinal atrophy.
Tests: HLA-B51, pathergy, inflammatory markers, thrombophilia, FA, flare photometry, brain imaging.

Treat: steroids + azathioprine (EULAR). Severe → + ciclosporin or infliximab (avoid ciclosporin with CNS disease). Infliximab/adalimumab early. Interferon-α (not with azathioprine). No anticoagulants.
chunks.hook: Behçet = B51, Bouts of ulcers, Both arteries and veins.

cards.q: Positive pathergy test?
cards.a: Sterile pustule 24–48 h after a needle prick (Behçet).

cards.q: How does Behçet vasculitis differ from sarcoid?
cards.a: Behçet involves arteries and veins (occlusive); sarcoid is mainly periphlebitis.

chunks.title: Toxoplasmosis: basics & signs
chunks.tldr: Commonest cause of focal retinitis. Cat = definitive host. Typical: fluffy white retinitis next to an old pigmented scar ('satellite'), dense vitritis → 'headlight in the fog'.
points: Toxoplasma gondii. Cat sheds oocysts → food/water/soil. Undercooked meat (bradyzoite cysts). Transplacental (active infection in pregnancy), transplant, transfusion.
Tachyzoites = active form. Bradyzoites = dormant in cysts (eye, brain, muscle).
Congenital: worse early in pregnancy, retinochoroiditis >75% (macular scars found later).
Acquired adults: 80–90% silent; lymph nodes, fever.
20–60% of posterior uveitis. Usually reactivation at the edge of an old scar. First symptoms ~age 29.
Symptoms: one eye, floaters, blur, photophobia.
Signs: spill-over AU (can be granulomatous, high IOP), single white focus + adjacent pigmented scar, posterior pole, vitritis ('headlight in fog'), vasculitis, disc oedema.
Atypical: multiple/new lesions and fulminant retinitis in the immunocompromised, neuroretinitis, punctate outer retinal toxoplasmosis.
Vision loss (~25%): macula/nerve involved, vessel occlusion, RD, late CNV.
Heals in 6–8 weeks → sharp atrophic scar with pigment rim. Recurrences ~2.7 per patient; >50% within 5 years.
chunks.hook: Headlight in the fog next to an old scar = toxo.

cards.q: Classic fundus appearance of reactivated toxoplasmosis?
cards.a: Fluffy white focal retinitis adjacent to an old pigmented scar with vitritis ('headlight in the fog').

cards.q: Definitive host of Toxoplasma gondii?

chunks.title: Toxoplasmosis: tests & treatment
chunks.tldr: Diagnose clinically (IgG supports, IgM = recent, PCR if unsure). Treat if near the macula/disc/big vessel, severe vitritis, or immunocompromised. Classic: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid (+ pred after 24–48 h). Alternatives: co-trimoxazole, intravitreal clindamycin + dex.
points: IgG = past exposure (common in population). IgM = infection within ~1 year (key in pregnancy).
PCR of aqueous/vitreous: specific, variably sensitive. Goldmann–Witmer coefficient (intraocular vs serum antibody).
OCT (CMO), B-scan (RD), FAF.
Self-limiting → treat only if sight-threatening: macula, papillomacular bundle, optic nerve, major vessel, severe vitritis, immunocompromised. 4–6 weeks.
Pyrimethamine 75–100 mg load → 25–50 mg daily + folinic acid (weekly FBC; caution in AIDS).
Sulfadiazine 1 g QID (stones, allergy, SJS).
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg only with antimicrobials (often after 24–48 h).
Intravitreal clindamycin 1 mg + dexamethasone 400 µg (2–3 injections): good for reactivation, pregnancy.
Co-trimoxazole BD (cheap, well tolerated). Azithromycin may reduce recurrences. Clindamycin (colitis), atovaquone.
Never depot steroids (triamcinolone) → uncontrolled spread.
Pregnancy: careful; spiramycin for new infection.
Immunocompromised → maintenance therapy.
chunks.hook: Toxo treatment: P-S-F (Pyrimethamine, Sulfadiazine, Folinic acid) ± Pred.

cards.q: Why give folinic acid with pyrimethamine?
cards.a: To prevent bone marrow suppression (it's a folate antagonist).

cards.q: Steroid formulation to avoid in toxoplasmosis?
cards.a: Depot periocular/intravitreal triamcinolone (risk of fulminant progression).

chunks.title: Toxocariasis
chunks.tldr: Dog roundworm (Toxocara canis), kids eating dirt. Eye: chronic endophthalmitis (leukocoria), posterior pole or peripheral granuloma with vitreous bands. Must exclude retinoblastoma.
points: Puppies shed eggs → children eat soil → larvae migrate.
Visceral larva migrans: age 2–7, fever, cough, liver, eosinophilia.
Ocular larva migrans: older kids/adults, one eye, low worm load, vision loss in ~2/3.
Chronic endophthalmitis: leukocoria, squint, uveitis, vitritis, peripheral snowbank-like exudate → tractional RD, phthisis.
Granuloma (1–2 DD, yellow-white) at the posterior pole or periphery, quiet eye, vitreous band to the disc → macular drag, RD.
Also chorioretinal scar, DUSN.
Tests: eosinophilia, IgE, serology (only ~50% in ocular cases), B-scan, aqueous/vitreous.
Treat: hygiene, deworm pets, steroids, albendazole/mebendazole (dying worms inflame), vitrectomy for traction.
chunks.hook: Puppy + white pupil → think toxocara, but rule out retinoblastoma.

cards.q: Main differential for a Toxocara granuloma in a child?

chunks.title: Onchocerciasis, cysticercosis, DUSN
chunks.tldr: River blindness = Onchocerca, blackfly, Africa → snowflake keratitis, sclerosing keratitis, chorioretinitis. Ivermectin yearly. Cysticercosis = pork tapeworm larva cyst. DUSN = one wandering subretinal worm → laser it.
points: Onchocerciasis: 2nd commonest infectious blindness. Simulium blackfly near fast rivers. Microfilariae from adult worms in nodules. Wolbachia symbiont.
Skin: itch, rash, 'leopard skin' on shins, onchocercomas (nodules). Eosinophilia.

Eye: live microfilariae in AC (after face-down posture), AU with pear-shaped pupil, snowflake punctate keratitis (3 & 9 o'clock) → sclerosing keratitis, temporal chorioretinitis/atrophy, optic neuritis.
Diagnose: skin snip, serology, oncho-dipstick, PCR.
Treat: ivermectin (kills microfilariae, yearly; careful with Loa loa → encephalopathy), moxidectin, doxycycline (kills Wolbachia), suramin (adults), steroids.

Cysticercosis: Taenia solium larva. Brain (neurocysticercosis). Eye: conjunctival/orbital cysts, floating AC cyst, subretinal/vitreous cyst (→ RD, severe inflammation when it dies). Steroids + surgical removal; albendazole carefully.

DUSN: single motile subretinal nematode. One eye, slow vision loss. Acute: crops of grey-white outer retinal spots, vitritis, papillitis. Late: optic atrophy, thin vessels, diffuse RPE loss. ERG reduced early.
DUSN treatment: laser the worm if seen (lure away from the fovea first), albendazole, vitrectomy.
chunks.hook: River blindness → Ivermectin yearly. DUSN → find the worm, laser it.

cards.q: Vector of onchocerciasis?
Why give doxycycline in onchocerciasis?
cards.a: It kills symbiotic Wolbachia, reducing microfilarial production.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for DUSN when the worm is visible?

chunks.title: HIV and the eye
chunks.tldr: AIDS = HIV + CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness. Commonest retinopathy: HIV microangiopathy (cotton-wool spots, harmless, fades) = warning sign for CMV retinitis.
points: Spread: sex, blood/needles, mother-to-child. Depletes CD4 T cells. ART for everyone.
Stages: flu-like seroconversion → latent (~8 years) → AIDS.
AIDS-defining: candidiasis, Pneumocystis, cryptosporidiosis, CMV retinitis, Kaposi, lymphomas, wasting, PML.
Lids: blepharitis, Kaposi, multiple mollusca, HZO.
Orbit: cellulitis (aspergillus), lymphoma.
Conjunctiva: Kaposi, SCC, microvasculopathy.
Cornea: dry eye, HSV/VZV/fungal keratitis.
AU from infections or drugs (rifabutin, cidofovir).
HIV microangiopathy (up to 70%): cotton-wool spots, haemorrhages, microaneurysms. No symptoms, fades in weeks. Marks low CD4 → CMV risk.
chunks.hook: HIV cotton-wool spots = harmless clouds that warn of the CMV storm.

cards.q: Commonest retinopathy in AIDS?
Two drugs causing anterior uveitis in HIV patients?

chunks.title: CMV retinitis
chunks.tldr: AIDS with CD4 <50. 'Pizza pie': white necrotic retina + flame haemorrhages along the arcades, little vitritis. Treat: ART + valganciclovir. RD in up to 50%. Watch for immune recovery uveitis.
points: Opportunistic, reactivated. Strongly tied to low CD4. Less common since ART.
Blur (macula) or floaters. One eye → 50% both if untreated. Indolent peripheral form can be silent.
Mild AU, mild vitritis (unless immune recovery).
Fulminant: dense white retina + haemorrhages ('pizza pie') along the vessels. Indolent: granular peripheral, few haemorrhages.
Optic neuritis. Frosted branch angiitis (~6%).
Healed areas: atrophy + holes → RD (up to 50%) → PPV + endolaser + silicone oil (~75% success).
Immune recovery uveitis: inflammation after ART restores immunity → vitritis, CMO, can → phthisis. Steroids carefully.

Treat with ID team: ART (stop anti-CMV when CD4 >100–150), valganciclovir 900 mg BD × 3 weeks → 900 mg daily (neutropenia → filgrastim). IV ganciclovir/foscarnet/cidofovir reserve. Ganciclovir implant (8 months).
Screen: CD4 <50 → 3-monthly, 50–100 → 6-monthly, >100 → yearly.
chunks.hook: CMV = 'pizza pie' in a very immunosuppressed patient, quiet vitreous.

cards.q: Typical CD4 count for CMV retinitis?
Oral drug for CMV retinitis induction and maintenance?

chunks.title: ARN vs PORN
chunks.tldr: ARN = healthy person, lots of inflammation (panuveitis, vitritis), peripheral necrosis spreading around, arteritis. PORN = AIDS, no inflammation, deep retinitis racing in, cherry-red spot. Both: VZV/HSV, high RD risk.
points: ARN: HSV in the young, VZV in older people. Can follow HSV encephalitis/skin infection.
ARN criteria (AUS): panuveitis (± scleritis), discrete peripheral necrosis with sharp edges, circumferential spread, occlusive vasculitis incl. arteritis, rapid progression. Painful.
ARN: heals in 6–12 weeks → necrotic retina → RRD; >50% end ≤6/60.

ARN treatment: IV aciclovir 15 mg/kg 8-hourly 10–14 days → oral 800 mg 5×/day for 6–12 weeks (or valaciclovir 2 g TDS → 1 g TDS). Protects the other eye. ± intravitreal ganciclovir/foscarnet. Oral steroids after 24 h. Prophylactic laser doesn't help. PPV + oil for RD.
PORN / PRN: usually VZV, AIDS or drug immunosuppression. Fast vision loss, one or both eyes.
PORN: minimal AU and vitritis. Deep yellow-white multifocal spots, early macula → cherry-red spot, spreads fast, little vasculitis/haemorrhage. RD, optic atrophy. >½ NPL.
PORN treatment: ART + aggressive IV + intravitreal ganciclovir/foscarnet.
Diagnosis: aqueous/vitreous PCR.
chunks.hook: ARN = Angry eye (healthy host). PORN = Peaceful eye, terrible prognosis.

cards.q: Necrotizing retinitis with minimal vitritis in AIDS, early macular cherry-red spot?
cards.a: Progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN), usually VZV.

cards.q: Main benefit of systemic aciclovir in ARN?
cards.a: Greatly reduces risk of second-eye involvement.

chunks.title: Viral anterior uveitis: HSV, VZV, CMV
chunks.tldr: All three: one eye, high IOP, iris atrophy. HSV = patchy atrophy. VZV = sectoral atrophy after shingles. CMV = white eye, high IOP, endotheliitis, doesn't respond to aciclovir → valganciclovir.
points: HSV AU: patchy (sometimes sectoral) iris atrophy incl. pigment layer, high IOP, bigger pupil, KPs fine/stellate or large. Same eye recurs. Treat: topical steroid + cycloplegic + oral aciclovir 400 mg 5×/day (or valaciclovir/famciclovir).

VZV AU: ~50% of HZO, starts 1–3 weeks after the rash (or zoster sine herpete). Sectoral iris atrophy, reduced corneal sensation, high IOP, can be granulomatous. Steroid + mydriatic + antiviral. Monitor HZO weekly for ≥6 weeks. Recurrence → aciclovir 800 mg 5×/day.

CMV AU (immunocompetent): recurrent or chronic, very high IOP (Posner–Schlossman can be CMV), little injection/flare, endotheliitis, sectoral atrophy, rarely synechiae. Fails aciclovir/steroids → aqueous PCR → oral valganciclovir (sometimes long-term).
Rubella: congenital (cataract, AU, salt-and-pepper retinopathy, glaucoma, microphthalmos); latent rubella → steroid-resistant CAU, Fuchs.
Measles: conjunctivitis, keratitis, retinitis; SSPE → posterior uveitis.
Mumps (rare iritis, IK), vaccinia, Zika (congenital macular atrophy), Ebola (uveitis in 1/3 of survivors).
chunks.hook: Viral AU triad: 1 eye, high IOP, iris holes.

cards.q: Clue that anterior uveitis may be CMV rather than HSV?
cards.a: Failure to respond to aciclovir/steroids; white eye, very high IOP, endotheliitis.

cards.q: Congenital rubella retinopathy appearance?

chunks.title: Histoplasmosis (POHS) & AIDS fungi
chunks.tldr: POHS triad: punched-out 'histo spots' + peripapillary atrophy + NO vitritis. Danger = CNV → anti-VEGF, Amsler the other eye. Pneumocystis = yellow-orange choroidal spots in AIDS.
points: Histoplasma capsulatum (inhaled; Mississippi/Ohio valleys). Eye disease = immune reaction. HLA-B7, DR2.
Usually symptom-free. 60% both eyes.
Triad: histo spots (~200 µm white atrophic), peripapillary atrophy, no vitritis. Linear midperipheral streaks (5%).
CNV (<5%) from a macular spot → 60% end <6/60 untreated → intravitreal anti-VEGF.
Macular histo spot → 25% CNV risk in that eye → weekly Amsler.
Pneumocystis jirovecii choroiditis (AIDS): multiple deep yellow-orange round lesions, little vitritis, vision OK.
Cryptococcus: multifocal choroiditis, or papilloedema/motility problems from meningitis.
chunks.hook: POHS: spots, ring round the disc, clear vitreous.

cards.q: Classic triad of POHS?
cards.a: Punched-out 'histo' spots, peripapillary atrophy, absence of vitritis.

cards.q: Main sight-threatening complication of POHS?

chunks.title: Endogenous Candida & Aspergillus
chunks.tldr: IV drug user / long-term line / diabetic → slow vitritis with 'cotton ball' or 'string of pearls' colonies + white chorioretinal spots → vitreous biopsy, voriconazole ± intravitreal, early PPV. Aspergillus is faster and hits the macula.
points: Candida albicans: risks = IV drug use, indwelling catheter, cystic fibrosis, debility, diabetes. (Uncommon in AIDS.)
Up to 1/3 of untreated candidaemia → eye involvement. Slow. Often bilateral.
Signs: fluffy 'cotton ball' / 'string of pearls' vitreous colonies, creamy chorioretinal lesions, necrosis → RD with PVR.
Tests: vitreous biopsy (cutter) for culture/PCR, blood/urine cultures.
Treat: voriconazole (good penetration) or amphotericin + flucytosine; intravitreal amphotericin/voriconazole; early vitrectomy.
Aspergillus: IV drugs, lung disease, transplant, neutropenia. Faster, early macular yellow infiltrates, occlusive vasculitis, worse outcome. Check for endocarditis.
Coccidioidomycosis: granulomatous AU + multifocal choroiditis.
chunks.hook: IV drugs + fluffy cotton balls in the vitreous = Candida.

cards.q: Typical vitreous appearance in Candida endophthalmitis?
cards.a: Fluffy 'cotton ball' or 'string of pearls' colonies.

cards.q: Which fungal endophthalmitis involves the macula earlier and progresses faster?

chunks.title: Tuberculous uveitis
chunks.tldr: Granulomatous AU with broad posterior synechiae, vitritis, choroidal tubercles, serpiginoid choroiditis, occlusive periphlebitis (Eales?). Test: IGRA (QuantiFERON), CXR. Treat with 4-drug ATT + steroids.
points: Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Eye disease often without obvious lung disease.
Granulomatous AU, iris nodules, broad posterior synechiae, vitritis, CMO, ERM.
Choroidal tubercles (dome-shaped, single/multiple); tuberculoma (big).
Serpiginoid choroiditis (spreading outward); choroiditis tracking vessels is fairly specific.
Occlusive periphlebitis → ischaemia → NV. Some Eales disease may be TB hypersensitivity.
Others: lupus vulgaris lids, phlyctenulosis, IK, scleritis, exudative RD, optic neuropathy.
Tests: tuberculin skin test, IGRA (not affected by BCG), sputum PCR, CXR/CT/PET, HIV test. Ocular PCR specific but often negative.

Treat: specialist multi-drug therapy (watch ethambutol optic neuropathy; rifabutin AU). Treating latent TB with uveitis halves recurrences. Steroids alongside (paradoxical worsening). Laser ischaemic retina.
chunks.hook: TB uveitis: think it in any granulomatous or serpiginous picture — QuantiFERON before steroids.

cards.q: Advantage of IGRA over tuberculin skin test?
cards.a: Not affected by previous BCG vaccination.

cards.q: TB drug needing visual monitoring?

chunks.title: Syphilitic uveitis
chunks.tldr: 'Great imitator'. Granulomatous or not, bilateral in 50%, iris roseolae, chorioretinitis, ASPPC (big yellow placoid macular lesion), ground-glass retinitis, optic neuritis. Treat as neurosyphilis (IV penicillin), test for HIV.
points: Treponema pallidum, usually sexual.
Stages: primary painless chancre → secondary maculopapular rash (palms/soles) → latent → tertiary (~40% untreated: aortitis, neurosyphilis, gummas).
AU in ~4% of secondary syphilis; 50% bilateral; roseolae (dilated iris capillaries → yellow nodules); high IOP.
Chorioretinitis (focal or multifocal, vitritis, exudative RD).
ASPPC (acute syphilitic posterior placoid chorioretinopathy): large pale-yellow placoid lesion at the posterior pole; more in immunosuppressed.
Ground-glass retinitis, occlusive vasculitis (arteries + veins) → diffuse scars.
Optic neuritis, neuroretinitis, IU, scleritis, Argyll Robertson pupils.
Tests: treponemal + RPR/VDRL, LP (neurosyphilis), HIV status, ocular PCR if serology unreliable.
Treat: parenteral penicillin (neurosyphilis regimen) with ID team ± steroids. Watch for Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction.
chunks.hook: Any weird uveitis → test for syphilis.

cards.q: Large pale-yellow placoid macular lesion in an HIV patient with uveitis?
Febrile reaction after starting penicillin for syphilis?

chunks.title: Lyme, brucella, endogenous bacteria, cat scratch, leprosy
chunks.tldr: Lyme: tick bite → erythema migrans → IU/neuro/CN VII palsy. Cat scratch (Bartonella) → neuroretinitis with macular star. Leprosy → iris pearls, beaded corneal nerves. Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis → septic, find the source.
points: Lyme (Borrelia burgdorferi, Ixodes tick, deer). Erythema chronicum migrans → neuro (CN palsies, meningitis), cardiac → arthritis, neuropathy.

Lyme eye: intermediate uveitis (commonest), AU, posterior/vasculitis, neuroretinitis; conjunctivitis (early), stromal keratitis, episcleritis, scleritis, myositis, optic neuritis, facial palsy (up to 25% in endemic areas).
Lyme Rx: doxycycline (not kids/pregnancy) / amoxicillin early; IV ceftriaxone/penicillin if established.
Brucellosis: unpasteurised milk. Chronic uveitis, papilloedema. Doxycycline + streptomycin.

Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis: septic patient (lines, IV drugs, joints, endocarditis). Early retinal infiltrates, then like post-op endophthalmitis. Mortality 5–10%. Cultures + IV antibiotics + intravitreal + PPV.

Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae): papule + lymphadenopathy. Eye 5–10%: neuroretinitis (disc swelling + macular star), retinochoroiditis, Parinaud oculoglandular. Doxycycline 4–6 weeks (erythromycin in kids).

Leprosy: tuberculoid → borderline → lepromatous (leonine face, digit loss). Eye: thick beaded corneal nerves, keratitis, pannus, plasmoid AU, small pupil + iris atrophy, iris pearls (pathognomonic), reduced corneal sensation, lagophthalmos (CN VII). Dapsone + rifampicin + clofazimine.
chunks.hook: Kitten scratch → star at the macula. Leprosy → pearls on the iris.

cards.q: Disc swelling + macular star after a cat scratch?
Pathognomonic iris sign of lepromatous leprosy?
Most common uveitis pattern in Lyme disease?

chunks.title: MEWDS, AIBSE & APMPPE
chunks.tldr: MEWDS: young woman, one eye, after flu, tiny grey dots + orange granular fovea, big blind spot, goes away by itself. APMPPE: both eyes, big creamy placoid lesions, FA dark early/bright late, beware cerebral vasculitis.
points: MEWDS: young women, viral prodrome in 25–50%. Painless one-sided blur + photopsia.
MEWDS signs: mild vitritis, many small (100–300 µm) grey-white deep dots sparing the fovea, orange granular foveal sheen, ± disc oedema.
MEWDS tests: enlarged blind spot, OCT ellipsoid disruption, FAF bright spots, FA early hyper/late stain ('wreath'), ICGA many dark spots, ERG reduced a-wave.
MEWDS: recovers in 2–6 weeks; 10% recur; no treatment (except CNV).
AIBSE: big blind spot + photopsia (maybe MEWDS variant).
APMPPE: young adults, viral prodrome 1/3, both eyes (second eye within weeks). Choriocapillaris inflammation → RPE ischaemia.
APMPPE signs: multiple large cream placoid lesions at the posterior pole → fade to RPE mottling. Headache/neuro symptoms (cerebral vasculitis → stroke).
APMPPE tests: FA early hypo, late hyper (blocked then stains), ICGA non-perfusion. HLA-B7/DR2. MRI/LP if neuro.
APMPPE: good prognosis usually (25% ≤6/15). Steroids if macula or CNS vasculitis.
chunks.hook: MEWDS = Mostly one Eye, Woman, Dots, Self-limiting. APMPPE = big Plaques, Pair of eyes, watch the brain.

cards.q: Characteristic foveal sign in MEWDS?
cards.a: Orange granular appearance with dulled foveal reflex.

cards.q: Serious systemic association of APMPPE?
FA pattern of active APMPPE lesions?

chunks.title: Serpiginous & related (RPC, PPM, AMN, AZOOR)
chunks.tldr: Serpiginous: middle-aged man, snake-like grey lesions spreading from the disc, recurrent → atrophy. Rule out TB ('serpiginoid'). AZOOR: young woman, zone of field loss, near-normal fundus, abnormal ERG.
points: Serpiginous choroidopathy: both eyes (asymmetric), men, middle age, HLA-B7. Outer retina + choriocapillaris.
Grey-white lesions starting peripapillary and creeping out in snake-like (serpiginous) tongues; macular variant 5%. Recur next to old scars → extensive atrophy.
Complications: CNV 15–35%, fibrosis, NV.
FA early hypo/late hyper; ICGA dark throughout.
Exclude TB. Treat: steroids + immunosuppressants/infliximab.
Relentless placoid (ampiginous): mix of APMPPE + serpiginous.
Persistent placoid maculopathy: like macular serpiginous but milder; CNV common.
Acute macular neuroretinopathy: young women (± flu, OCP), paracentral scotomas, red-brown wedge-shaped petal lesions round the fovea, recovers.

AZOOR: young/middle-aged women, sudden zonal field loss (often temporal), photopsia, fundus nearly normal early → later RPE clumping. ERG: reduced a/b, delayed 30 Hz; EOG reduced. Stabilises in 6 months mostly.
chunks.hook: Serpiginous = snake slithering out from the disc.

cards.q: Where does serpiginous choroidopathy typically start?
cards.a: Around the optic disc (peripapillary), spreading outward.

cards.q: Key test in AZOOR with a near-normal fundus?

chunks.title: PIC, MCP & SFU ('pseudo-POHS')
chunks.tldr: Young myopic women. PIC = small yellow spots at the macula, no inflammation, CNV up to 40%. MCP = spots everywhere + AU/vitritis, chronic. SFU = progressive subretinal fibrosis.
points: Punctate inner choroidopathy: young myopic women, both eyes sequentially. Blur, floaters, photopsia.
PIC: little/no AU or vitritis. Small yellow-white fuzzy macular spots (inner choroid) → sharp punched-out scars (like histo spots).
PIC: CNV up to 40% → anti-VEGF; steroids/immunosuppression for recurrent disease.
Multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis: young-middle aged women, chronic/recurrent, both eyes.

MCP: AU (50%) + vitritis, multiple 50–350 µm yellow-grey spots at the pole/periphery, linear streaks, pigmented scars, peripapillary atrophy. CNV 25–35%, CMO, fibrosis. Field defects bigger than expected.
MCP FA: early hypo/late hyper; ICGA many dark spots.
MCP treatment: steroids → immunosuppression; CNV → steroids + anti-VEGF.
SFU: very rare, myopic young women, AU + vitritis + subretinal mounds → widespread subretinal fibrosis. Poor prognosis.
chunks.hook: PIC = Pure macular spots, no inflammation. MCP = Many spots + Cells.

cards.q: Main threat to vision in PIC?
How does MCP differ from PIC?
cards.a: MCP has anterior uveitis/vitritis and spots beyond the macula.

chunks.title: Birdshot retinochoroiditis
chunks.tldr: Middle-aged (often white) woman, HLA-A29 (>95%), vitritis + cream ovoid choroidal spots radiating from the disc, sparing the macula. Monitor with visual fields + ERG, not VA. Needs long-term immunosuppression.
points: Chronic, bilateral. Retinitis and choroiditis behave separately.
Slow central blur, photopsia, floaters (often more symptoms than VA suggests).
Vitritis. Many ill-defined cream ovoid spots <1 DD in the pole/midperiphery, radiating out from the disc. Old ones = atrophic spots.
Complications: CMO, ERM, CNV.
Monitor with visual fields (and ERG), not acuity.
Tests: HLA-A29, OCT, FAF (more spots), FA (vessel and disc leakage, diffuse oedema; fovea often spared), ICGA (more dark spots early), ERG (rod/cone loss over time).
~1/3 end <6/60 historically; better with aggressive treatment.
Treat: sub-Tenon triamcinolone (one eye) → systemic (up to 90%): steroids → mycophenolate → infliximab.
chunks.hook: Birdshot = A29 ('a shotgun with 29 pellets').

cards.q: HLA association of birdshot?
Best functional test for monitoring birdshot?
cards.a: Visual fields (and ERG), not visual acuity.

chunks.title: Rare ones: ARPE, AIM, FBA, IRVAN & more
chunks.tldr: ARPE = clusters of grey spots with yellow haloes at the macula, recovers. AIM = grey exudative macular detachment → bull's eye. Frosted branch angiitis = florid vessel sheathing. IRVAN = arteriolar aneurysms + neuroretinitis → laser ischaemic retina.
points: ARPE (Krill): young adults, one eye, mild blur; 2–4 clusters of small grey RPE spots with yellow haloes; resolves 6–12 weeks; EOG low.
Acute idiopathic maculopathy: young adults, flu prodrome, sudden central loss; grey-yellow exudative macular detachment, small haemorrhages, papillitis → may leave a bull's eye.
Acute multifocal retinitis: multiple retinitis spots, macular star (maybe Bartonella).
Solitary idiopathic choroiditis: single yellow choroidal elevation, vitritis; steroids if sight-threatening.
Frosted branch angiitis: florid white sheathing of arterioles + venules. Primary (kids/young, both eyes, steroid-responsive, good prognosis) or secondary (CMV, lymphoma, leukaemia).
IRVAN: young women. Arteritis + multiple arteriolar aneurysms (incl. on the disc) + neuroretinitis, exudates, peripheral non-perfusion → NV → early PRP; anti-VEGF/steroids.
chunks.hook: IRVAN = Idiopathic Retinal Vasculitis, Aneurysms, Neuroretinitis.

cards.q: What does IRVAN stand for?
cards.a: Idiopathic Retinal Vasculitis, Aneurysms and Neuroretinitis.

cards.q: Name 2 secondary causes of frosted branch angiitis.
